name: Tanmaxxing with peptides

lead: Peptide tanning means using synthetic analogues of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, mainly melanotan II, to stimulate melanin production. The aim is a darker tan with less sun exposure, which looksmaxxing communities associate with a healthier, more defined look.

The peptides act on melanocortin receptors in the skin. Melanotan I became the licensed drug afamelanotide for a rare light-sensitivity disorder; melanotan II has never been approved, and unlicensed products circulate online.

paras: Users in these communities describe injectable products obtained from unlicensed sellers, usually combined with some sun or sunbed exposure to develop colour. No dosing or sourcing is given here.

Health agencies in Denmark, the UK, Ireland, Norway and the US have warned about unlicensed melanotan products, citing legality, case reports and possible impurities. Reported effects include flushing, nausea, vomiting, yawning, appetite loss and darkening of moles and freckles.

angle.text: The peptides stimulate melanin production, which darkens skin. Users pursue this as an alternative or supplement to UV tanning.

lead: Tanmaxxing with peptides is the practice of using melanocortin peptides, chiefly melanotan II, to darken the skin. Melanotan II is a synthetic analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone that stimulates melanin production and so produces tanning [1].

The compounds originate from University of Arizona researchers who sought sunless tanning agents in the 1980s, creating melanotan I and melanotan II. Melanotan I became afamelanotide, licensed to the Australian company Epitan (later Clinuvel); melanotan II was licensed to Palatin Technologies as a sexual-dysfunction treatment, and Palatin stopped developing it in 2000 [1][2].

Afamelanotide, sold as Scenesse, was approved in Italy in 2010, by the EMA in 2015 and by the US FDA in 2019 for erythropoietic protoporphyria, as an implant [2]. Melanotan II has never been approved, and health agencies have warned against unlicensed products since 2007 [1].
infobox: Melanotan II unapproved; agency warnings since 2007 [1]

paras: Afamelanotide binds the melanocortin 1 receptor, driving melanogenesis. It resists breakdown more than the natural hormone but has a short half-life of about 30 minutes [2].

Listed effects of melanotan II include flushing, nausea, vomiting, stretching, yawning, appetite loss and spontaneous erections in men, plus reversible darkening of moles and freckles. Case reports describe significant safety risks [1].

Whether it affects melanoma risk is unclear: a 2013 review found no conclusive evidence of causation, and a 2021 review attributed higher melanoma rates among users to heavy UV exposure and sun-seeking behaviour [1]. Unlicensed products are sold online and in some gyms and salons, and agencies in Denmark, the UK, Ireland, Norway and the US have warned against them, citing legality, case reports and potential impurities [1].
No studies found for peptide tanning as an appearance practice.
Related trials of licensed afamelanotide for erythropoietic protoporphyria, including three trials of 244 adults that supported FDA approval, concern light tolerance rather than cosmetic tanning [2].

timeline.event: Palatin Technologies stops developing melanotan II [1].
Health agencies begin issuing warnings about unlicensed melanotan [1].
